newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: AUSTRALIAN TELECOMMUNICATIONS GROWTH SEEN SLOWING.
newsitem.headline: AUSTRALIAN TELECOMMUNICATIONS GROWTH SEEN SLOWING.

text.p: Revenue growth in Australia's telecommunications market is set to slow in calendar 1997 to seven percent after double digit growth for most of the decade, a telecommunications analyst said on Tuesday.

Paul Budde, of consultants Paul Budde Communication Pty Ltd, said in a report that prices in phone services were falling due to more competition following deregulation on July 1. But the overall market volume was still growing, he said.
Budde said prices for fixed line calls were set to drop by between 40 to 80 percent, mobile calls by between 30 and 50 percent and pay television by 25 percent.
He said new market entrants would also entice customers with free local call and Internet access.

Budde said that although revenue growth would slow, Australia's telecom market volume would grow by between 10 and 20 percent in the 1997 year, cellular phones by 30 to 40 percent and data services, including the Internet, by between 40 and 100 percent. "However, this growth no longer compensates for the drop in prices forced upon the players by competition," he said.
"We forecast a five percent revenue growth for the industry over 1997. The situation for 1998 will not be much better."
Australia's A$25 billion telecommunications market is dominated by state-owned Telstra Corp and number two player Optus Communications Pty Ltd.

Budde said Telstra would only be able to boost profitability through efficiency gains as Optus and other players would continue to eat into its market by up to five percent per year for the next few years. "With most infrastructure plans abandoned for the time being, the long-term future for Telstra looks bleak," Budde said.
The government plans to sell a third of Telstra in a public share offer this year, potentially raising over A$10 billion.

Telstra announced last month that it would stop the rollout of its A$4.0 billion cable network following a planned merger between its 50 percent owned pay TV arm, Foxtel, and satellite TV operator Australis Media Ltd.

Budde said new players would be able to develop their own infrastructure to deliver the revenues able to be derived from the range of new high-speed Internet and video based services, which would come available from around 2000-2003.
By 2006, the converged telecommunications/broadcasting and entertainment market would have grown to about A$75 billion, the report said.
Australia has one of the world's highest penetration rates of mobile phones, but price falls are likely to keep market revenue around A$3.0 billion, Budde said.
